los.text: Identify the legal requirements of investment companies.
Compare the method of capitalization and pricing of open-end and closed-end investment companies.
Contrast the mutual fund share classes and relate them to the different types of loads.
Identify the characteristics of private funds and venture capital funds.
Identify the structure, compensation arrangements, and suitability requirements of a hedge fund.
Recall the special features of unit investment trusts.
Identify the distinguishing characteristics of exchange-traded funds (ETFs).
Identify the unique features of real estate investment trusts (REITs).
Explain the benefits and risks of pooled investments in client portfolios.

concepts.subtopic: Three types under the 1940 Act; board composition
concepts.explanation: An investment company pools investors' money into a diversified, professionally managed portfolio; it registers under the Securities Act of 1933 and is regulated by the SEC under the Investment Company Act of 1940. The Act names three types: face-amount certificate companies (issuer promises a fixed sum at a future date for lump-sum or installment payments — only testable fact: it is one of the three), management investment companies (open-end = mutual funds, and closed-end), and unit investment trusts. Holding companies are NOT investment companies. Net asset value per share = (assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding. A management company's board may be no more than 60% interested persons — at least 40% must be noninterested (outside) directors.
rules: Three types: FAC companies, management companies (open-end/closed-end), UITs.
Max 60% interested directors; ≥40% outside directors.
Holding companies are excluded from the definition.
formulas: NAV per share = (total assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding
misconceptions: Listing growth or income funds as 'types' of investment company — those are objectives, not legal classifications.

concepts.subtopic: Prohibited activities, shareholder votes, contracts, affiliated persons, custody, redemption, reports
concepts.explanation: Mutual funds may not buy on margin, sell short, join a joint trading account, or own more than 3% of another investment company's voting securities (they must issue common stock — that is their ownership form). A majority vote of outstanding shares is needed for fundamental changes (open-end↔closed-end, diversified↔nondiversified, change of objective, ceasing to be an investment company) and to approve the adviser and underwriter contracts. Those contracts must be written, state all compensation, be renewed annually after two years by the board or shareholders, be terminable on no more than 60 days' written notice without penalty, and be approved by a majority of noninterested directors. Minimum net worth to offer publicly: $100,000. Affiliated persons (5%+ owners, control persons, officers, directors, employees; control = more than 25%) may not sell personally owned securities to the fund (except redeeming fund shares), borrow from the fund, or buy anything from the fund except its shares. Assets must be held by a custodian (usually a bank — FDIC coverage not required — or an exchange-member broker-dealer). Redemption proceeds within 7 days at the next computed NAV. Annual audited reports to the SEC; shareholders get financial information semiannually.
rules: No margin, no short sales, no joint accounts, ≤3% of another fund.
Advisory contract: written, annual renewal after 2 years, ≤60 days' termination notice, approved by outside directors.
Affiliated person = 5%+; control person = >25%.
Redemption within 7 days; reports to shareholders semiannually.
exceptions: A broker-dealer may extend margin credit on fund shares the customer has owned more than 30 days (Exchange Act 11(d)(1) exemption).
examples: A fund's principal underwriter may buy and redeem the fund's shares but may not buy securities out of the fund's portfolio.
misconceptions: Believing an affiliated person can borrow from the fund with enough asset coverage — never permitted.
Thinking the custodian bank must be FDIC-insured.

concepts.explanation: Open-end funds (mutual funds) make a continuous primary offering of an unlimited number of common shares — every purchase is a new issue, so a prospectus must be delivered before or during the solicitation; they issue common stock only, allow fractional shares, and must redeem shares at NAV (capital shrinks on redemptions). Closed-end funds (publicly traded funds) do one fixed offering through underwriters, may also issue preferred stock and bonds, do not redeem, and trade in the secondary market (exchange or OTC) in full shares only at a price set by supply and demand — at a premium or discount to NAV, which they compute only about weekly. Country funds are usually closed-end because foreign holdings are hard to liquidate.
rules: Open-end: unlimited shares, common only, fractional shares, redeemable at NAV, price = NAV + sales charge (never below NAV).
Closed-end: fixed capitalization, may issue preferred and debt, full shares, not redeemable, price = market ± commission, can be above/below/at NAV.
misconceptions: Thinking a closed-end fund's price is tied to NAV.
Confusing what an open-end fund may issue (common only) with what it may invest in (bonds are fine).

concepts.explanation: A mutual fund's public offering price (POP) = NAV + sales charge. NAV is computed at least daily as of the market close (4:00 pm ET). Forward pricing: every purchase or redemption order gets the next computed NAV — an order received before 4:00 pm gets that day's close; at 4:00 pm or later, the next business day's. Shares can be fractional, so investors think in dollars: $100 at a $15 NAV buys 6.667 shares.
rules: POP = NAV + sales charge.
Next computed price after the order is received (forward pricing).
formulas: Shares bought = dollars ÷ price per share
misconceptions: Assuming an order is filled at the last computed price.

concepts.subtopic: Front-end, back-end (CDSC), 12b-1; expense ratio; Classes A, B, C, I, R
concepts.explanation: FINRA caps sales charges at 8.5% of POP; the sales charge is always stated as a percent of POP, not NAV ($10 POP, $9.50 NAV → 5%). Three ways distributors collect: front-end load (Class A — added to NAV at purchase; lowest operating expenses), back-end load / contingent deferred sales charge (Class B — declining percentage on redemption, e.g. 8%, 7%, 6%…, reaching zero in 6–8 years, then converting to A), and 12b-1 asset-based fees (Class C level load — no front charge, usually a 1% CDSC for one year, ongoing 12b-1; for exam purposes C shares do not convert to A). 12b-1 fees pay only marketing/distribution, never portfolio management; must be reasonable (max 0.75% of average net assets), under a written plan approved initially by a majority of shares and annually by the board including outside directors, terminable by outside directors or shareholders; a fund charging more than 0.25% cannot call itself no-load. Class I = institutional (lower fees); Class R = retirement plans (no loads, modest 12b-1). Expense ratio = annual operating expenses (management fee + operating expenses) ÷ average net assets; the sales charge is not included; aggressive funds have higher ratios. Rights are identical across classes.
rules: Max sales charge 8.5% of POP.
12b-1: max 0.75%; >0.25% → not 'no-load'; marketing only.
B shares convert to A after 6–8 years; C shares do not (exam).
exceptions: Commission-free ETF platforms and C→A conversions exist in practice but are not the exam default.
formulas: Expense ratio = operating expenses ÷ average net assets
examples: Expense ratio 1.72% = $1.72 per year per $100 invested.
misconceptions: Computing the load as a percent of NAV.
Counting the sales charge in the expense ratio.

concepts.subtopic: Breakpoints, breakpoint sales, letter of intent, rights of accumulation, combination/exchange privileges
concepts.explanation: Class A sales charges fall at breakpoints (declining schedule by amount invested). 'Any person' eligible: married couples, parents and minor children, corporations — not investment clubs or siblings. A breakpoint sale — selling just under a breakpoint to earn a bigger commission without telling the client — violates just and equitable principles; large B-share purchases also draw scrutiny. Letter of intent: a one-sided promise (binding on the fund only) to reach a breakpoint within 13 months; extra shares are escrowed until completed; appreciation and reinvested dividends don't count; may be backdated up to 90 days (still 13 months total); if not completed the investor pays the difference or escrowed shares are sold. Rights of accumulation: on subsequent purchases, prior holdings (valued at the higher of cost or current NAV), no commitment, no time limit, appreciation counts. Combination privilege: aggregate purchases across funds in the same family. Exchange (conversion) privilege: switch funds within a family at NAV without a new load — but every exchange is a taxable sale.
rules: LOI: 13 months, forward-looking, backdate ≤90 days, escrowed shares, appreciation excluded.
ROA: no time limit, subsequent purchases, appreciation counts.
Exchanges within a family avoid loads but are taxable events.
exceptions: Investment clubs never qualify for breakpoints.
examples: $24,000 order with a $25,000 breakpoint: the rep must mention that $1,000 more saves 1% ($250).
LOI signed 60 days after the first purchase leaves 11 months.
misconceptions: Thinking a letter of intent binds the investor — it binds only the fund.
Letting appreciation count toward an LOI (it counts for ROA, not LOI).

concepts.subtopic: 3(c)(1) and 3(c)(7) exemptions; private equity, liquidity funds, venture capital; 2-and-20
concepts.explanation: Private (private equity) funds avoid investment-company registration either with no more than 100 investors (3(c)(1)) or with any number of qualified purchasers — individuals with $5 million in investments, entities with $25 million (3(c)(7)). Usually partnerships; long holding periods (hedge funds trade actively by contrast). Direct-investment funds take 10%+ voting stakes to influence operating companies; portfolio funds build noncontrol portfolios. Private liquidity funds mimic money market funds while escaping the 2014 MMF rules (less disclosure). Venture capital funds are limited partnerships (GP decides, LPs supply capital — wealthy individuals, pensions, endowments, even hedge funds) that back young, not-yet-operational companies seeking an exit within 10 years. PE and VC managers typically earn 2% of committed capital plus 20% of profits (carried interest).
rules: 3(c)(1): ≤100 investors. 3(c)(7): qualified purchasers only ($5M individuals / $25M entities).
VC = pre-operating start-ups; PE/hedge = going concerns.
Compensation: 2 and 20 (carried interest).
examples: An entrepreneur with no operating history should approach a venture capital fund.
misconceptions: Sending a start-up to a hedge fund or mutual fund — they buy marketable securities of going concerns.

concepts.subtopic: Structure, strategies, fees, lock-ups, suitability, funds of funds
concepts.explanation: Hedge funds are usually limited partnerships with no more than 100 investors, unregistered with the SEC (their managers generally must register as investment advisers); offered by private placement memorandum, so little transparency. They may use arbitrage, heavy short selling, leverage, options and futures — strategies mutual funds cannot — aiming for positive returns in all markets while reducing volatility (no assurance). Fees are high: '2 and 20' (2% management + 20% of profits), sometimes with a hurdle rate the fund must beat before the incentive fee. Lock-up provisions bar withdrawals for an initial period, making them illiquid; even afterward there is no secondary market and GP approval may be needed to sell interests. High minimums (commonly $500,000–$1 million) and risk limit them to institutions and accredited investors. Managers invest alongside ('skin in the game'); the partnership issues the units. Funds of hedge funds (minimums as low as $2,500) offer diversification but layered fees and little added liquidity (7-day redemption rule waived). What hedge funds and mutual funds share: both are pooled investments.
rules: LP, ≤100 investors, unregistered, PPM.
2 and 20; hurdle rate; lock-up.
Accredited investors only; high minimums.
exceptions: Fund of funds lets ordinary investors in but adds a second layer of fees.
examples: A policy barring withdrawals for the first 6 months is a lock-up period; a 60-day notice requirement is not.
misconceptions: Promising a hedge fund will profit in up and down markets — that is the goal, not a guarantee.

concepts.explanation: A UIT is an unmanaged investment company organized under a trust indenture: no board of directors (trustees instead), no investment adviser, no management fee, no active trading. It issues redeemable units (shares of beneficial interest) representing an undivided interest in a fixed portfolio chosen to meet a stated objective — e.g., a municipal bond trust that liquidates when the last bond matures, or an equity trust liquidated at a set date (proceeds paid out or rolled into a new trust). Trustees must maintain a secondary market so units can be redeemed at NAV. Some ETFs are organized as UITs.
rules: Unmanaged; no BOD, no adviser, no management fee.
Units must be redeemed by the trust.
It is an investment company under the 1940 Act.
misconceptions: Saying a UIT's board of directors oversees it — it has none.

concepts.explanation: ETFs register under the 1940 Act as UITs or open-end companies (most are open-end, but cannot be called mutual funds because shares are not redeemable). Most track an index (any liquid asset class with an index — stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities); actively managed ETFs exist. Like an index fund in holdings, like a closed-end fund in trading: priced intraday on an exchange, can be bought on margin and sold short, generally lower expense ratios, tax advantages (rarely distribute capital gains). Small premiums/discounts to NAV arise from late-day trading and normally close at the next open (unlike closed-end funds' persistent gaps). Drawback: commissions on each trade make ETFs less suitable than no-load index funds for small periodic investments (dollar cost averaging), except on commission-free platforms. Neither an ETF nor an index fund can be expected to beat its index — expenses see to that.
rules: Trades like a stock: intraday, margin, short.
Lower expenses, tax-efficient.
Not ideal for small recurring purchases because of commissions.
exceptions: Commission-free proprietary ETFs on some platforms — the exception for exam purposes.
examples: Investor wants sector exposure on margin with no year-end capital gains statements → sector ETF, not a sector mutual fund.
misconceptions: Claiming an ETF outperforms its index.

concepts.explanation: A REIT manages a portfolio of real estate to produce income and/or gains; shares trade on exchanges or OTC (not redeemable) — assume publicly traded unless told otherwise (nontraded REITs have limited liquidity and stricter suitability). Types: equity (own property), mortgage (hold mortgages), hybrid. Tax: a corporation that avoids corporate tax under Subchapter M if it invests at least 75% of assets in real estate and cash, derives at least 75% of gross income from real estate (rents, mortgage interest), and distributes at least 90% of taxable income as dividends. Dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income (not qualified); capital gains distributions at long-term rates. REITs are NOT investment companies and NOT DPPs — they pass through income and gains but not losses.
rules: 75% assets / 75% income / 90% distribution.
Not an investment company; not a DPP (no loss pass-through).
Dividends taxed as ordinary income.
exceptions: Nontraded REITs: limited liquidity, redemption offers may be below purchase price.
misconceptions: Calling a REIT a mutual fund or expecting it to flow through losses.

concepts.explanation: All pooled vehicles offer diversification (the number-one advantage of mutual funds) and professional management (fund managers must be SEC-registered advisers following the prospectus objective). Mutual funds add: choice of objectives (growth, income, capital preservation via money market funds, growth-and-income, sector funds with ≥25% in one industry or region), convenience, liquidity (redeem at next NAV, paid within 7 days), low minimums, simplified taxes (Form 1099), combination and exchange privileges. Risks: market risk (equity funds), interest-rate risk (bond funds have no maturity date, unlike a bond); only money market funds hold a stable price but their income varies and is uninsured; fees (sales charges, 12b-1, redemption fees, management fees — the largest ongoing cost); no control over the manager's timing, so tax efficiency suffers; net redemptions in falling markets force sales at bad prices. Compare funds on services, costs, taxation, management tenure, and performance versus an appropriate benchmark, net of all expenses. Permissible claims: diversification and professional management — not better performance, tax advantages, or lower expenses than DIY investing.
rules: Benefits: diversification, professional management, choice, convenience, liquidity, low minimums, tax reporting, family privileges.
Risks: market/interest-rate risk, fees, tax inefficiency, net redemptions.
exceptions: Money market fund prices don't fluctuate, but income is variable and not FDIC-insured.
misconceptions: Telling a client mutual funds outperform individual stocks or offer special tax advantages.

concepts.subtopic: Private funds, hedge funds and REITs: benefits and risks
concepts.explanation: Private funds: chance for very large profits by investing before an IPO, a say in management, low correlation to the market; risks — business risk (most start-ups fail), liquidity risk (no secondary market; post-IPO shares likely restricted), no regulatory review (lack of transparency). Hedge funds: designed for positive returns in rising and falling markets, many styles, may lower portfolio volatility and add uncorrelated returns; risks — high expenses, strategies can backfire, lock-ups and no secondary market, GP approval to transfer. REITs: real estate exposure without direct-ownership illiquidity, professional selection with negotiating power, negative correlation with stocks, income and appreciation; risks — dependence on management quality, more price volatility than direct real estate, nonqualified dividends taxed as ordinary income, nontraded REITs are illiquid, losing REIT status means corporate tax, problem loans hurt mortgage REITs. Two strategies hedge funds use that mutual funds cannot: buying on margin and selling short.
rules: Hedge vs. mutual fund: margin and short selling are hedge-fund only.
REIT dividends: ordinary income; REIT shares trade — liquid when listed.
misconceptions: Describing hedge fund shares as easy to redeem.

lessons.title: Investment companies and the 1940 Act rulebook
lessons.objective: Name the three types of investment company, state the board-composition rule, and recall what funds and their affiliates may not do, what shareholders must vote on, and the custody, redemption and reporting requirements.

blocks.b:
An **investment company** pools money from many investors into a large, diversified portfolio run by professionals. It sells shares under the **Securities Act of 1933** (registration and prospectus) and is regulated by the SEC under the **Investment Company Act of 1940**.

The 1940 Act names **three types**:
- **Face-amount certificate companies** — the issuer promises a fixed sum at a future date in exchange for lump-sum or installment payments. The only testable fact: it is one of the three.
- **Management investment companies** — actively managed portfolios, either **open-end (mutual funds)** or **closed-end**.
- **Unit investment trusts** (Lesson 3.5).

**Holding companies are not investment companies.** Growth funds, income funds and the like are *objectives*, not legal types.

**NAV per share** = (assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding — the basis for pricing open-end funds, and much less relevant for closed-end funds.

A management company's board may be **no more than 60% interested persons** — equivalently, **at least 40% must be noninterested ('outside') directors**, people whose only tie to the fund is the board seat (and maybe some shares). No one is 'interested' merely for sitting on the board or owning shares.

blocks.h: What a mutual fund may not do
What shareholders vote on; the adviser's contract

blocks.b:
An **affiliated person** owns or controls **5% or more** of the shares, or is an officer, director, partner, employee, or under common control (a **control person** owns **more than 25%**). Affiliates and underwriters may not **sell personally owned securities to the fund** (redeeming fund shares is fine), **borrow from the fund** (never — no amount of asset coverage changes that), or **buy anything from the fund except its shares**.

- **Custody**: assets stay with a **custodian** — usually a bank (FDIC coverage **not** required) or an exchange-member broker-dealer.
- **Redemption**: proceeds within **7 days** at the next computed NAV.
- **Reports**: audited annual financials to the SEC; financial information to shareholders **semiannually**.

lessons.title: Open-end vs. closed-end: how shares are created, priced and traded
lessons.objective: Contrast the capitalization, securities issued, share types, trading venue and pricing of open-end and closed-end funds, and apply forward pricing.

blocks.b: A **mutual fund** registers an **open offering** and issues new shares continuously — every purchase is a **primary offering** with the money going to the fund, so a **prospectus must be delivered before or during the solicitation**. It issues **common stock only** (what it *invests* in is a different matter — a bond fund sells common shares and buys bonds). Shares can be **fractional**, so investors think in dollars. When you sell, the fund **redeems** at NAV and its capital shrinks.

blocks.h: Closed-end: one offering, then the secondary market
blocks.b: A **closed-end fund** ('publicly traded fund') registers a **fixed** number of shares, sells them once through underwriters like any IPO, and may also issue **preferred stock and bonds** — a capital structure like any corporation. Afterward shares trade on an **exchange or OTC** in **full shares only**, with bid and ask set by **supply and demand** — at a **premium or discount to NAV**. NAV has so little bearing on price that it's typically computed only **weekly**. **Country funds** (Korea Fund, Mexico Fund) are usually closed-end because foreign holdings are hard to liquidate.

rows: Bought from / redeemed by the fund (primary)
Secondary market, exchange or OTC; not redeemed
NAV + sales charge — never below NAV
Market price ± commission — above, below or at NAV

blocks.b: A fund's **POP = NAV + sales charge**. NAV is computed at least **once a day at the close (4:00 pm ET)**. Every order to buy or redeem gets the **next computed NAV** after it arrives: before 4:00 pm → today's close; at or after 4:00 pm → tomorrow's close. At a $15 price, $100 buys 6.667 shares.

lessons.title: Loads, share classes, and how to pay less
lessons.objective: Explain front-end, back-end and 12b-1 charges and Classes A/B/C/I/R, compute a sales charge and expense ratio, and apply breakpoints, letters of intent, rights of accumulation and family privileges.

blocks.h: Three ways to pay the distributor
blocks.b:
FINRA caps mutual fund sales charges at **8.5% of the POP**. The load is always a **percent of POP, not NAV**: POP $10, NAV $9.50 → the 50¢ load is **5%**.

- **Front-end load** — added to NAV when you buy. **Class A**. Lowest ongoing expenses.
- **Back-end load / CDSC** (contingent deferred sales charge) — charged on redemption on a **declining schedule** (8%, 7%, 6%…), hitting zero after 6–8 years, when the shares **convert to Class A**. **Class B**.
- **12b-1 asset-based fee** — an annual percentage of average net assets for **marketing and distribution only** (never portfolio management). **Class C** ('level load'): no front charge, usually a 1% CDSC for the first year, ongoing 12b-1; for the exam, **C shares do not convert to A**.

Other letters: **Class I** = institutional (lower fees); **Class R** = retirement plans (no loads, a 12b-1 between A and B/C). Voting and other rights are identical across classes.

A 12b-1 fee needs a **written plan** approved initially by a **majority of outstanding shares** and reapproved **annually by the board including the outside directors**; it can be terminated by the outside directors or the shareholders. The fee must be reasonable — **max 0.75%** of average net assets — and if it exceeds **0.25%** the fund **cannot call itself no-load**.

**Expense ratio** = management fees + operating expenses ÷ average net assets. 1.72% means $1.72 a year per $100 invested. The **sales charge is not an expense** in this ratio. Every fund has one, load or no-load, and aggressive funds (more trading) run higher.

Class A funds publish **breakpoints** — a declining sales-charge schedule by amount invested (e.g., 6.5% under $25,000, 5.5% to $50,000 … 0% at $1 million). 'Any person' may use them: **married couples, parents with minor children, corporations** — but **not investment clubs** or, say, siblings pooling money.

A **breakpoint sale** — taking a $24,000 order without telling the client that $1,000 more would save $250 — violates just and equitable principles of trade. Regulators also frown on **large Class B purchases**: at breakpoint size, A shares' lower expenses win within a few years, and most firms refuse B-share orders over $100,000.

blocks.h: Letter of intent vs. rights of accumulation
blocks.b:
**Letter of intent (LOI)**: the investor promises to reach a breakpoint within **13 months**. One-sided — **binding on the fund only**. Each purchase gets the reduced charge immediately; the extra shares are held in **escrow** until the letter is completed. **Appreciation and reinvested dividends do not count.** May be **backdated up to 90 days** to capture earlier purchases, but the whole window is still 13 months (sign after 60 days → 11 months left). Miss the target → pay the difference or the escrowed shares are sold.

**Rights of accumulation (ROA)**: on **subsequent** purchases, prior holdings — valued at the **higher of cost or current NAV** — count toward the breakpoint. **No commitment, no time limit, appreciation counts.**

**Combination privilege**: add up holdings across funds in the same **family**. **Exchange (conversion) privilege**: move between family funds at NAV with no new load — but **every exchange is a taxable sale**.

lessons.title: Private funds, venture capital and hedge funds
lessons.objective: State the 3(c)(1)/3(c)(7) exemptions, distinguish private equity, liquidity and venture capital funds, and describe hedge fund structure, strategies, fees, lock-ups and suitability.

blocks.b:
**Private (private equity) funds** avoid being investment companies two ways:
- **3(c)(1)**: no more than **100 investors**.
- **3(c)(7)**: unlimited investors, but all must be **qualified purchasers** — individuals with **$5 million** in investments, entities with **$25 million**.

They're usually **partnerships** and hold investments for the long run (hedge funds, a special kind of private fund, trade actively). **Direct-investment** funds take **10%+ voting stakes** in operating companies to influence management; **portfolio** funds build noncontrol portfolios. **Private liquidity funds** copy money market funds while dodging the 2014 MMF rules — less disclosure.

**Venture capital funds** are limited partnerships (the **GP decides, LPs fund** — wealthy individuals, pensions, endowments, even hedge funds) that back **young, not-yet-operating** companies, aiming for an exit within **10 years**. An entrepreneur with no operating history goes to a VC fund — PE and hedge funds want going concerns, mutual funds want marketable securities.

PE and VC managers typically earn **2% of committed capital plus 20% of profits** — the **carried interest**.

- **Structure**: usually a **limited partnership**, **≤100 investors**, **not registered** with the SEC (managers generally register as advisers). Offered by **private placement memorandum** — far less disclosure than a prospectus, so **little transparency**.
- **Strategies** off-limits to mutual funds: arbitrage, large **short** positions, **leverage**, options and futures. Goal: positive returns in all markets with lower volatility — a goal, not a promise.
- **Fees**: '**2 and 20**' — 2% management plus 20% of profits — sometimes only above a **hurdle rate** (e.g., 4%).
- **Lock-up**: no withdrawals for an initial period (say one year); even afterward there's no secondary market and the GP may have to approve a transfer. Illiquid.
- **Suitability**: institutions and **accredited investors**; minimums commonly **$500,000–$1 million** (some $25,000, some $25 million) — the high minimum is why they suit few investors. Managers have **skin in the game**; the partnership issues the units.
- **Fund of hedge funds**: minimums as low as $2,500, diversification across managers, but **layered fees** and no real liquidity gain (the 7-day redemption rule is waived).

What a hedge fund and a mutual fund have in common: both are **pooled investments**. Not transparency, not low cost, not liquidity.

lessons.title: UITs, ETFs and REITs
lessons.objective: Recall the defining features of unit investment trusts, exchange-traded funds and real estate investment trusts, including the REIT 75/75/90 tests.

blocks.b: The third 1940-Act type. A UIT is **unmanaged**, organized under a **trust indenture**: **no board of directors** (trustees instead), **no investment adviser**, **no management fee**, no trading. It issues redeemable **units** (shares of beneficial interest) in a **fixed portfolio** built to a stated objective — a municipal bond trust that dissolves when the last bond matures, or an equity trust liquidated on a set date (cash out or roll into a new trust). The trustees must maintain a secondary market so units can be **redeemed at NAV**. Some ETFs are UITs.

An ETF registers under the 1940 Act as a **UIT** or an **open-end company** (most are open-end — but they can't be called mutual funds because shares aren't redeemable). Most **track an index** (anything liquid with a published index: stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities); actively managed ETFs are growing.

Holdings like an index fund; trading like a closed-end fund: **intraday on an exchange**, can be **bought on margin and sold short**, generally **lower expense ratios**, and **tax-efficient** (rarely distribute capital gains). Small premiums/discounts from late-day trading normally close at the next open — unlike a closed-end fund's persistent gap.

Drawback: **commissions each way**, so for small recurring investments (dollar cost averaging) a **no-load index fund** usually beats an ETF — except on commission-free platforms, which are the exam's exception.

Neither an ETF nor an index fund can claim to **beat its index** — the index has no expenses.

A **REIT** runs a portfolio of real estate for income and/or gains: **equity** REITs own property, **mortgage** REITs hold mortgages, **hybrids** do both. Shares trade on **exchanges or OTC** — **not redeemable**; assume publicly traded unless told otherwise (nontraded REITs are illiquid and need stricter suitability).

Tax: a REIT is a corporation but escapes corporate tax under **Subchapter M** by meeting three numbers:
- **75%** of assets in real estate and cash
- **75%** of gross income from real estate (rents, mortgage interest)
- **90%** of taxable income distributed as dividends

Those dividends are generally **ordinary income** (not qualified); capital gains distributions get long-term rates.

Four exam points: an undivided interest in a real estate pool; **liquid** because they trade; **not investment companies**; **not DPPs** — income and gains pass through, **losses do not**.

lessons.title: Why — and why not — to put pooled investments in a portfolio
lessons.objective: Articulate the benefits and risks of mutual funds, private funds, hedge funds and REITs in client portfolios, and name what may and may not be claimed about mutual funds.

blocks.b:
Every pooled vehicle offers **diversification** and **professional management** — diversification is generally agreed to be the **number one** advantage of mutual funds. Managers must be SEC-registered advisers who follow the prospectus objective.

More pluses: **choice of objectives** (aggressive growth to conservative, income from governments to high yield, capital preservation via money market funds, growth-and-income, **sector funds** with at least 25% in one industry or region); **convenience**; **liquidity** (redeem at next NAV, paid within 7 days); **low minimums** (often $100 for additions); **simple tax reporting** (Form 1099); **combination** and **exchange** privileges within a family (exchanges are still taxable).

What you may *not* claim: better performance than individual securities, special tax advantages, or lower expenses than do-it-yourself investing. Investors still must match the fund to their goals and read the prospectus.

- **Market risk** in equity funds; **interest-rate risk** in bond funds — and unlike a bond, a bond fund **never matures**.
- Only the **money market fund** holds a stable price, at the cost of little growth, low and **variable** income, and no FDIC insurance (unlike a bank CD).
- **Fees**: sales charges, 12b-1, redemption fees, and the **management fee** — usually the largest ongoing cost. The prospectus won't capture every cost; compare **net returns after expenses and taxes**.
- **Tax inefficiency**: you don't control when the manager realizes gains.
- **Net redemptions**: in a falling market, redemptions exceed purchases and the manager must sell into weakness.

Compare similar funds on services, costs, taxation, **management tenure** (a qualitative factor), and **performance versus the right benchmark**.

**Private funds** — for: very large profits possible by investing pre-IPO, a say in management, low correlation to the market. Against: **business risk** (most start-ups fail), **liquidity risk** (no secondary market; post-IPO shares likely restricted), **no regulatory review**.

**Hedge funds** — for: designed to profit in up and down markets, many styles, may reduce portfolio volatility, uncorrelated returns. Against: **high expenses**, strategies that can backfire, **lock-ups** and no secondary market, GP approval to transfer. Two tools hedge funds use that mutual funds can't: **margin** and **short selling**.

**REITs** — for: real estate without direct ownership's illiquidity, professional selection with negotiating clout, **negative correlation** with the stock market, income plus appreciation. Against: dependence on management quality, **more price volatility** than direct real estate, **dividends taxed as ordinary income**, illiquidity if **nontraded**, corporate tax if the distribution tests are missed, and problem loans in mortgage REITs.

questions.stem: Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, the three classifications of investment company are
options: growth funds, income funds, and balanced funds.
face-amount certificate companies, management companies, and unit investment trusts.
open-end companies, closed-end companies, and holding companies.
mutual funds, hedge funds, and REITs.
questions.explanation: The Act classifies investment companies as face-amount certificate companies, management investment companies (open-end and closed-end), and unit investment trusts.
why: Those are investment objectives, not legal classifications.
Holding companies are specifically excluded; open- and closed-end are subtypes of management companies.
Hedge funds and REITs are not investment companies.

questions.stem: A management investment company's board of directors has 10 members. The maximum number who may be interested persons is
questions.explanation: No more than 60% of the board may be interested persons, so at least 40% (4 of 10) must be noninterested; 6 interested is the maximum.
why: Four is the minimum number of outside directors.
A simple majority is not the test.
At least 40% must be outside directors.

questions.stem: A registered open-end investment company is permitted to
options: purchase portfolio securities on margin.
issue common stock to raise capital.
sell securities short.
own 10% of the voting shares of another mutual fund.
questions.explanation: Issuing common stock is how a mutual fund is owned and capitalized. Margin purchases, short sales, joint accounts, and holding more than 3% of another investment company are prohibited.
why: Margin purchases are prohibited.
Short sales are prohibited.
The limit is 3% of another investment company's voting securities.

questions.stem: Which statement about a mutual fund's contract with its investment adviser is correct?
options: It may be oral if approved by the board.
It must be renewed annually after the first two years and be terminable on no more than 60 days' written notice without penalty.
It requires approval only of the interested directors.
It may be terminated only by a vote of the shareholders.
questions.explanation: Advisory contracts must be written, describe compensation, be renewed annually after two years by the board or shareholders, be terminable on no more than 60 days' notice, and be approved by a majority of noninterested directors.
why: The contract must be in writing.
Approval by the noninterested (outside) directors is required.
The board or the shareholders may terminate it.

questions.stem: An officer of the XYZ Fund owns a block of ABC Corp. bonds that he believes would fit the fund's portfolio. Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, he
options: may sell them to the fund at the current market price.
may sell them to the fund only with board approval.
may not sell personally owned securities to the fund.
may lend them to the fund instead.
questions.explanation: Affiliated persons (officers, directors, 5%+ owners, etc.) may not sell personally owned securities to the fund, borrow from it, or buy anything from it other than its own shares.
why: Prohibited regardless of price.
Board approval does not cure the prohibition.
Affiliates may not engage in such transactions with the fund.

questions.stem: Which of the following may issue preferred stock and bonds in addition to common stock?
options: An open-end investment company
A closed-end investment company
A unit investment trust
A money market fund
questions.explanation: Closed-end funds can have a capital structure like any corporation: common, preferred and debt. Open-end funds issue only common stock; UITs issue units.
why: Open-end funds may issue common stock only.
UITs issue redeemable units of beneficial interest.
A money market fund is an open-end fund — common only.

questions.stem: A client owns shares of a fund that trade on the NYSE at $18.40 while the fund's reported NAV is $20.10. This fund is most likely
options: an open-end fund selling at a discount to NAV, which is prohibited.
a closed-end fund trading at a discount to NAV.
a unit investment trust.
a no-load mutual fund.
questions.explanation: Only closed-end funds trade on exchanges at supply-and-demand prices that may be above or below NAV. Open-end shares are never sold below NAV.
why: Open-end funds don't trade on exchanges and can't sell below NAV.
UIT units are redeemed by the trust at NAV.
Mutual funds are priced at NAV (plus any load), not on an exchange.

questions.stem: Because a mutual fund is a continuous primary offering, a prospectus must be delivered to a prospective investor
options: within 7 days after the purchase.
before or during any sales solicitation.
only if the purchase exceeds $25,000.
only on the first purchase in a fund family.
questions.explanation: Mutual fund shares are always a new issue, so the prospectus must precede or accompany any solicitation.
why: Delivery after the sale is too late.
No dollar threshold applies.
Each fund is a separate issuer.

questions.stem: A mutual fund computes NAV once daily at 4:00 pm ET. A redemption order received at 4:15 pm on Tuesday is priced at
options: Tuesday's 4:00 pm NAV.
Monday's 4:00 pm NAV.
Wednesday's 4:00 pm NAV.
the average of Tuesday's and Wednesday's NAV.
questions.explanation: Forward pricing: an order receives the next NAV computed after it is received. After the 4:00 pm cutoff, that is the next business day's close.
why: The order arrived after that computation.
Prices are never backward-looking.
No averaging is used.

questions.stem: A mutual fund's NAV is $14.25 and its public offering price is $15.00. The sales charge is
questions.explanation: Sales charge = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP = $0.75 ÷ $15.00 = 5%.
why: That divides by NAV; the charge is a percent of POP.
Arithmetic error.
That is the dollar amount, not a percent.

questions.stem: Which statement about 12b-1 fees is correct?
options: They may be used to pay the fund's portfolio manager.
A fund whose 12b-1 fee exceeds 0.25% of average net assets may not describe itself as no-load.
They are deducted from the investor's purchase at the time of sale.
They are included in the fund's sales load calculation.
questions.explanation: 12b-1 fees are annual asset-based charges for marketing and distribution only; a fund charging more than 0.25% cannot call itself no-load. The maximum is 0.75%.
why: 12b-1 money never pays for portfolio management.
They are ongoing annual charges, not a point-of-sale deduction.
They are technically not a sales load (though called an asset-based sales charge).

questions.stem: Compared with Class A shares of the same fund, Class B shares
options: have a front-end load and lower expenses.
have a contingent deferred sales charge that declines over time and higher ongoing expenses until they convert to Class A.
never convert to Class A shares.
are available only to institutional investors.
questions.explanation: Class B shares carry a declining back-end load (CDSC) and higher 12b-1 expenses; after 6–8 years the load reaches zero and they convert to Class A.
why: Class A carries the front-end load.
For exam purposes, Class C shares don't convert; B shares do.
Class I shares are institutional.

questions.stem: A fund's expense ratio
options: includes the front-end sales charge.
is calculated by dividing annual operating expenses by average net assets.
is zero for no-load funds.
is typically higher for a Treasury bond fund than for an aggressive growth fund.
questions.explanation: Expense ratio = management fees and operating expenses ÷ average assets under management; sales charges are excluded; all funds have one, and aggressive funds tend to be higher.
why: Sales charges are not operating expenses.
No-load funds still have management and operating expenses.
More trading in aggressive funds raises their ratios.

questions.stem: A fund's breakpoints reduce the sales charge at $50,000. An IAR places a $48,000 Class A purchase for a client without mentioning the breakpoint. This is
options: acceptable because the client did not request the breakpoint.
a breakpoint sale, considered contrary to just and equitable principles of trade.
acceptable if the client signs a letter of intent later.
a violation only if the IAR is also a broker-dealer agent.
questions.explanation: Selling just below a breakpoint without disclosing the savings is a breakpoint sale, prohibited by state and federal regulators.
why: The obligation to disclose does not depend on the client asking.
The violation occurs at the time of the undisclosed sale.
Both state and federal rules apply to anyone selling fund shares.

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of rights of accumulation but NOT of a letter of intent?
options: There is a 13-month time limit.
Share appreciation counts toward reaching the breakpoint.
Shares purchased at the reduced charge are held in escrow.
The investor must commit to a specific future investment.
questions.explanation: Rights of accumulation value prior holdings at the higher of cost or current NAV, so appreciation counts, with no time limit or commitment. LOIs have a 13-month limit, escrowed shares, and exclude appreciation.
why: That is an LOI feature.
Escrow applies to LOIs.
LOIs state an intended amount; ROA requires no commitment.

questions.stem: All of the following statements about a letter of intent are correct EXCEPT
options: it may be backdated up to 90 days.
it is binding on the investor, who must complete the purchases.
reinvested dividends do not count toward the stated amount.
shares representing the sales-charge reduction are held in escrow until the letter is completed.
questions.explanation: An LOI is a one-sided contract binding only on the fund. If the investor fails to complete it, the escrowed shares cover the higher sales charge — there is no obligation to invest.
why: True — up to 90 days, within 13 months total.
True — only new money counts.
True — escrowed shares are released on completion.

questions.stem: To rely on the Section 3(c)(7) exclusion from the definition of investment company, a private fund must
options: have no more than 100 investors.
sell only to qualified purchasers.
register its interests with the SEC.
hold at least 75% of its assets in real estate.
questions.explanation: 3(c)(7) has no investor limit but requires all investors to be qualified purchasers ($5 million in investments for individuals, $25 million for entities). The 100-investor limit is 3(c)(1).
why: That is the 3(c)(1) exclusion.
The exclusion avoids registration.
That is a REIT test.

questions.stem: A biotech start-up with a promising compound but no revenues and no operations seeks financing. The most likely source is
options: a venture capital fund.
a hedge fund.
an open-end investment company.
a private liquidity fund.
questions.explanation: Venture capital funds invest in businesses not yet fully operational, accepting high risk for potentially high returns with an exit planned within about 10 years.
why: Hedge funds trade marketable securities of going concerns.
Mutual funds buy marketable securities.
Liquidity funds hold short-term obligations for stable value.

questions.stem: The typical compensation of a private equity or venture capital fund manager is best described as
options: a 12b-1 fee of up to 0.75% of net assets.
a 2% management fee plus 20% of profits (carried interest).
a front-end load of up to 8.5%.
a flat salary approved by the limited partners.
questions.explanation: Private equity, venture capital and hedge fund managers commonly receive about 2% of committed capital annually plus 20% of profits — the carried interest.
why: 12b-1 fees are mutual fund distribution charges.
Sales loads apply to mutual funds.
Managers are compensated through fees and carry, not a salary set by LPs.

questions.stem: Hedge funds are most commonly organized as
options: open-end management companies.
corporations.
limited partnerships.
unit investment trusts.
questions.explanation: Hedge funds are typically limited partnerships (≤100 investors) that avoid SEC registration; the managers usually invest alongside the limited partners.
why: Open-end companies are registered mutual funds.
Partnership form is used mainly for legal reasons.
UITs are unmanaged registered investment companies.

questions.stem: A hedge fund's offering document states that new investors may not withdraw capital during their first 12 months. This provision is
options: a hurdle rate.
a lock-up period.
a carried interest.
a redemption notice requirement.
questions.explanation: A lock-up provision bars withdrawals during an initial period, retaining capital for the manager and adding liquidity risk for the investor.
why: A hurdle rate is the return the fund must exceed before incentive fees are paid.
Carried interest is the manager's profit share.
A notice requirement (e.g., 60 days) is different from a prohibition.

questions.stem: A hedge fund and a mutual fund share which of the following characteristics?
options: Both must register with the SEC.
Both offer daily liquidity.
Both are pooled investments.
Both are limited to accredited investors.
questions.explanation: The common feature is pooling investors' money. Hedge funds are unregistered, illiquid during lock-ups, and limited to accredited investors.
why: Hedge funds are not registered.
Hedge funds have lock-ups and no secondary market.
Mutual funds are available to the public.

questions.stem: An IAR explaining hedge funds to a client should state that
options: interests are easy to redeem at any time.
the fund is guaranteed to profit in both rising and falling markets.
expenses, including performance fees, are typically much higher than those of mutual funds.
the fund must file a prospectus with the SEC.
questions.explanation: Hedge funds typically charge '2 and 20' with much higher total expenses; profits in all markets are an objective, not a guarantee; interests are illiquid; and they are offered by private placement memorandum.
why: Lock-ups and the lack of a secondary market make redemption difficult.
No investment outcome can be guaranteed.
Hedge funds are unregistered and use a PPM.

questions.stem: Which statement about a unit investment trust is NOT correct?
options: It is supervised by a board of directors.
Its portfolio is fixed once assembled.
It must redeem its units.
It is an investment company under the 1940 Act.
questions.explanation: A UIT has trustees, not a board of directors, and no investment adviser or management fee; it is unmanaged, redeemable, and a registered investment company.
why: True — no active trading.
True — trustees maintain a market and redeem at NAV.
True — one of the three types.

questions.stem: An investor owns units of a trust holding 30 municipal bonds that will terminate when the last bond matures, with no manager trading the portfolio. This is
options: a closed-end fund.
a unit investment trust.
a face-amount certificate company.
an exchange-traded note.
questions.explanation: A fixed, unmanaged portfolio that self-liquidates as bonds mature is the classic municipal bond UIT.
why: Closed-end funds are actively managed and trade on exchanges.
FAC companies promise a fixed sum at a future date.
ETNs are debt securities, not pooled portfolios.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a typical index ETF?
options: It may be purchased on margin.
It is priced throughout the trading day.
Its shares are redeemed by the fund at the next computed NAV.
Its expense ratio is generally lower than that of a comparable mutual fund.
questions.explanation: ETF shares trade on exchanges in the secondary market; they are not redeemed at NAV by the fund the way mutual fund shares are.
why: ETFs can be margined and shorted like stocks.
ETFs trade intraday.
Index-matching keeps ETF expenses low.

questions.stem: A client wants broad exposure to the energy sector, wants to use margin, and wants to minimize annual capital gains distributions. The most suitable choice is
options: an energy sector mutual fund.
an energy sector ETF.
shares of the two largest oil companies.
a hedge fund specializing in energy.
questions.explanation: ETFs can be bought on margin and rarely distribute capital gains, while providing diversified sector exposure. Mutual funds cannot be margined and distribute gains; two stocks aren't diversified.
why: Mutual funds can't be bought on margin and make taxable gains distributions.
Two stocks give poor sector representation.
Hedge funds have high minimums, lock-ups, and are for accredited investors.

questions.stem: An investor plans to invest $200 every month for 20 years. Compared with a no-load index mutual fund tracking the same index, an ETF is generally
options: more suitable because it trades intraday.
less suitable because brokerage commissions on each purchase erode small periodic investments.
more suitable because ETFs outperform their index.
equally suitable because both are redeemed at NAV.
questions.explanation: Each ETF purchase incurs a commission (absent a commission-free platform), making it less competitive than a no-load index fund for dollar cost averaging.
why: Intraday trading is irrelevant to a monthly saver.
Neither product can be expected to beat its index.
ETFs are not redeemed at NAV; they trade.

questions.stem: To avoid taxation as a corporation, a REIT must distribute at least what portion of its taxable income to shareholders?
questions.explanation: Subchapter M requires a REIT to distribute at least 90% of taxable income; 75% figures apply to assets and income from real estate.
why: Too low.
75% is the asset and income test.
Full distribution is not required.

questions.stem: Which statement about publicly traded REITs is correct?
options: They are registered investment companies under the 1940 Act.
They pass through operating losses to shareholders like a limited partnership.
Their dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income rather than as qualified dividends.
Shares are redeemed by the trust at net asset value.
questions.explanation: REIT dividends are mostly nonqualified (ordinary income). REITs are not investment companies, do not pass through losses (so are not DPPs), and their shares trade rather than being redeemed.
why: REITs are not investment companies.
Losses do not flow through.
REIT shares trade on exchanges or OTC.

questions.stem: A REIT that owns office buildings and also holds commercial mortgages is classified as
options: an equity REIT.
a mortgage REIT.
a hybrid REIT.
a nontraded REIT.
questions.explanation: Equity REITs own property, mortgage REITs hold mortgages, and hybrids do both.
why: Equity REITs only own property.
Mortgage REITs only hold mortgages.
Nontraded refers to liquidity, not holdings.

questions.stem: When describing the advantages of mutual funds to a client, an IAR may properly cite
options: superior performance compared with individual securities.
diversification and professional management.
tax advantages unavailable to direct investors.
lower total expenses than self-directed investing.
questions.explanation: The two primary, defensible advantages are diversification and professional management. Performance, tax, and cost superiority cannot be claimed.
why: Performance can't be promised.
Fund investors have less control over taxable events.
Management fees can make funds more expensive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a risk specific to investing in a bond mutual fund rather than an individual bond?
options: The fund has no maturity date at which principal is returned.
The fund's income is guaranteed by the FDIC.
The fund cannot be redeemed.
The fund is exempt from interest-rate risk.
questions.explanation: An individual bond returns par at maturity; a bond fund has no maturity, so there is no date on which principal is assured. Bond funds remain subject to interest-rate risk and are redeemable.
why: No mutual fund is FDIC-insured.
Open-end funds must redeem shares.
Bond funds carry interest-rate risk.

questions.stem:
Which two strategies may a hedge fund use that a registered mutual fund may not?
I. Concentrating in a single industry
II. Buying portfolio securities on margin
III. Purchasing low-rated bonds
IV. Selling stock short
options: I and III
I and IV
II and III
II and IV
questions.explanation: The 1940 Act prohibits mutual funds from margin purchases and short sales; sector concentration and junk bonds are permitted to funds with that objective.
why: Sector funds concentrate; high-yield funds buy low-rated bonds.
Concentration is allowed for mutual funds.
Low-rated purchases are allowed.

questions.stem: An adviser recommends REITs to a client to add real estate exposure. A reason supporting this recommendation is that REITs
options: pay qualified dividends taxed at a maximum 15% rate.
tend to have a negative correlation with the general stock market.
flow through depreciation losses to offset the client's other income.
are redeemable at NAV on demand.
questions.explanation: Real estate and stock prices often move in opposite directions, so REITs can diversify a stock portfolio. REIT dividends are ordinary income, losses don't pass through, and shares trade rather than being redeemed.
why: REIT dividends are generally not qualified.
REITs are not DPPs; losses stay in the trust.
REIT shares trade in the secondary market.

questions.front: Three types of investment company; max % of interested directors
questions.back: Face-amount certificate companies, management companies (open-end/closed-end), UITs. No more than 60% interested (≥40% outside directors). Holding companies excluded.

questions.front: Four things a mutual fund may not do; affiliated vs. control person
questions.back: No margin, no short sales, no joint trading accounts, no more than 3% of another investment company. Affiliated = 5%+ owner; control = >25%.
Set by supply and demand on an exchange/OTC — can be above, below or at NAV. Open-end price = NAV + load, never below NAV.
Orders get the next computed NAV after receipt; NAV is computed at least daily at the 4:00 pm ET close.

questions.front: Max sales charge; max 12b-1; no-load threshold; sales charge formula
questions.back: 8.5% of POP; 12b-1 max 0.75% (over 0.25% → not no-load); sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP.

questions.front: LOI time limit and backdating; who qualifies for breakpoints
questions.back: 13 months, backdated up to 90 days, binding on fund only, appreciation excluded. Breakpoints: individuals, spouses, parents + minor children, corporations — not investment clubs.
3(c)(1): ≤100 investors. 3(c)(7): all qualified purchasers — $5M (individual) / $25M (entity) in investments.

questions.front: Hedge fund: structure, fees, liquidity, investors
questions.back: Limited partnership, ≤100 investors, unregistered (PPM). '2 and 20', maybe a hurdle rate. Lock-up periods. Accredited investors; high minimums.
No board of directors (trustees), no investment adviser, no management fee, no active trading. Units redeemable at NAV. Is an investment company.

questions.front: ETF vs. index mutual fund: three ETF advantages, one drawback
questions.back: Intraday trading, margin/short selling, lower expenses and tax efficiency. Drawback: commissions make small periodic purchases costly.
75% of assets in real estate/cash; 75% of income from real estate; distribute 90% of taxable income. Dividends = ordinary income. Not an investment company, not a DPP.

questions.front: Number-one advantage of mutual funds; is an exchange within a family taxable?
questions.back: Diversification (with professional management close behind). Yes — any exchange is a sale for tax purposes.

questions.front: Two strategies hedge funds use that mutual funds cannot
questions.back: Buying on margin and selling short.

terms.def: Annual asset-based charge for marketing and distribution; max 0.75%; over 0.25% disqualifies 'no-load'.
Owner of 5%+ of a fund's shares, or its officers, directors, employees or control persons; control = more than 25%.
Purchase level at which a Class A sales charge declines.
The manager's share of profits (typically 20%) in private equity, venture capital and hedge funds.
Declining back-end load on Class B (and briefly Class C) shares, charged at redemption.
Operating expenses ÷ average net assets; excludes sales charges.
Orders execute at the next NAV computed after receipt.
Minimum return a hedge fund must earn before the incentive fee applies.
Investor's 13-month promise to reach a breakpoint; binding on the fund only; shares escrowed.
Period during which a hedge fund investor may not withdraw capital.
NAV plus sales charge — the price at which mutual fund shares are bought.
Individual with $5 million or entity with $25 million in investments; eligible for 3(c)(7) funds.
Counting prior holdings (at higher of cost or NAV) toward a breakpoint on later purchases; no time limit.
Tax code section letting REITs (and funds) avoid corporate tax by distributing income; REIT test 75/75/90.
